clinician.trajectory_summary: The patient, a 55-year-old male with a history of prolonged intravenous heroin addiction, presented with bilateral hip pain, claudication, decreased muscle power, and soreness of lower limbs. Initial imaging revealed bilateral femoral neck insufficiency fractures and sacral ala insufficiency fractures. Whole-body bone scan showed multiple hot spots. Biochemical workup showed elevated alkaline phosphatase, decreased phosphate, calcium, 25-(OH)D3, and elevated urinary phosphate. DEXA confirmed osteoporosis with T scores of -3.2 spine and -4.0 hips. Labs showed decreased testosterone and normal thyroid and osteocalcin. No corticosteroid use, alcohol consumption, or other common osteoporosis risk factors were reported. The patient underwent bilateral hip hemiarthroplasty, and was treated with vitamin D3, calcium supplementation, and detoxification therapy. Six months later, biochemical markers normalized, supporting response to treatment and metabolic bone disease recovery. The clinical picture supports heroin-induced osteoporosis as the cause of bilateral femoral neck insufficiency fractures after exclusion of other common causes.
